newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: FEATURE - E.Timor's tourism potential ignored.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - E.Timor's tourism potential ignored.

text.p: Unspoilt beaches, a serene sea and clear blue skies -- at first glance, the landscape of East Timor might seem like a tourist's dream.
The territory's vistas are not unlike those on Bali, Indonesia's famed resort island 1,200 km (700 miles) to the west.
But there is one glaring difference: Bali brims with tourists; East Timor has only a handful if any at all.
Residents are astonished when asked about the discrepancy.

They say they have lived so long in a climate of fear spawned by Indonesia's 1975 invasion of East Timor, its formal annexation of the territory the next year and two decades of a guerrilla movement for self-determination that low tourist arrivals are far down on their list of priorities.

"No restaurants, no hotels can grow in such an environment," says Florentino Sarmento, the head of a local agricultural development programme. "The problem is democracy and it is profoundly affecting economic lives."
Often, the few waterfront eateries in Dili, the capital of East Timor, are deserted, and the occasional journalists the only foreign visitors. On its beaches, stray dogs outnumber fun-seekers.

By contrast, in Bali, dinner reservations are a must in the island's hundreds of packed restaurants. In the bars, Australian and German accents dominate conversation while the beaches are generously sprinkled with haute couture bikinis.
Bali streets are a cacophonous tangle of motorcycles and buses, but usually the only vehicles on East Timor's roads after dusk are military trucks moving in convoys.

Some five million foreign tourists visited Indonesia in 1996, about 1.5 million of them going on to Bali. In East Timor, the former Portuguese colony occupying half of the island of Timor, 1996 tourist arrivals totalled only 900.
UNREALISED POTENTIAL
"There is a lot of potential but it hasn't been developed yet," said Budi, an official at the almost-deserted tourism office in Dili.
Roads linking Dili to other parts of East Timor are poor, there is little public transport and telephone lines are hazy at best.
The political uncertainty also casts a gloom over commerce.
Residents and human rights groups say between 200,000 and 250,000 people were killed in the 1975 invasion, a subsequent famine and the two decades that Jakarta has tried to put down the insurrection.
Despite the unrest, there are no restrictions on travel. Foreigners visiting Indonesia do not need special permission to go to East Timor and two daily flights link the territory to Bali and Jakarta.

Budi said the main tourist attractions on East Timor were the giant statue of Christ the King overlooking Dili Bay, a memorial to Australian soldiers killed in World War Two in the hills south of Dili and facilities for swimming and snorkelling.
The south coast of Timor island, which Budi said was good for surfing, is almost entirely undeveloped.
Atauro, a small island about an hour's ride by ferry north of East Timor, is wonderfully scenic but there are no regular facilities to accomodate visitors, he said.
CLIMATE OF FEAR
Residents say the climate of fear which pervades East Timor is not conducive to tourism or indeed to any business activity.

"There are no industries here," says Salvador Soares, one of the four members of parliament from East Timor and a local leader of Indonesia's ruling Golkar party. "There are promises of investment, but nothing has come."

Unemployment among the 850,000 East Timorese is rife. Only small patches of land between the sea and the island's bleak hills are cultivable and these are given over to rice paddies. There is no evidence of sustained industrialisation.

According to government statistics, East Timor ranks lowest on a scale of human development among Indonesia's 27 provinces. There has been some success with a coffee plantation scheme aided by the U.S. government and an animal husbandry project but the benefits have been limited.

Government officials say Jakarta is aware of the problem. The government follows a policy of actively promoting development in the eastern provinces, which include East Timor, and earmarks special funds for that purpose.

President Suharto said during a visit to East Timor in October that per capita income in the province was 600,000 rupiah ($250) in 1994 compared with 80,000 rupiah in 1976. He said there were 2,100 km (800 miles) of roads in the territory in 1994 compared with just 51 km (30 miles) in 1976.
But clearly much needs to be done.
"All the small and medium businesses, they have left because now and then there is violence," says development official Sarmento.
"Tourism is even worse. No tourists are coming," he said.
